blocks.x: Medical and dental spaces are demanding commercial renovations. Patients need privacy and accessibility, clinicians need efficient workflow, and the space has to meet code and stand up to frequent cleaning. A clinic that's poorly planned costs time every single day. Good medical clinic design starts with the layout, long before finishes are chosen.
Medical clinic layout: start with patient and staff flow
Map how people move through the clinic before drawing walls:
**Arrival:** entrance, reception and waiting
**Intake:** check-in, triage or vitals
**Treatment:** exam rooms or operatories
**Support:** sterilization, labs, storage, staff areas
**Exit:** checkout and booking
Ask your clinical lead and designer how patient routes should be kept apart from utility routes, and keep staff steps short between exam rooms and support areas.
Key design questions for your clinical lead and designer

Clinical and infection-control rules come from your professional standards, your health authority and your own policies, not from your contractor. Settle these points with your clinical lead and designer before pricing. A contractor builds to their drawings and to your equipment supplier's specifications.

head: Area
What to settle with them
rows: How consistent should the layouts be, where do handwashing sinks go, and what lighting and sound privacy does each room need?
How should instruments move through the room, and how many dedicated sinks does your team need?
Which flooring, wall finishes and counters suit your cleaning products and policies?
Which rooms need sinks, and how far are they from existing lines?
Which equipment needs dedicated circuits, and does the emergency lighting change?
What air changes and temperatures do your rooms need?
Barrier-free entrance, washroom and doors as the [Manitoba Building Code](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/current/078-2023.php?lang=en) requires. Consider at least one accessible exam room.
Where do walls and doors need sound insulation, and how discreet should reception be?

blocks.x: **Dental clinics** add compressed air, vacuum and specialized plumbing to each operatory, and imaging rooms may need shielding as specified by the equipment supplier or a qualified expert.
Permits and approvals

Most medical office renovations in Winnipeg require a City of Winnipeg building permit, applied for with the City's [Commercial Alteration Design Summary](https://www.winnipeg.ca/media/6330) (CADS) form, plus plumbing, electrical and mechanical permits for that work, which [City-licensed contractors apply for](https://www.winnipeg.ca/building-development/building-renovating/commercial-projects).
The CADS form asks for an Electrical Patient Care Areas Declaration where treatment, diagnosis, therapy, monitoring or care of people takes place, so mark every care room on the floor plan.

If the space was previously used for something else, such as retail or general office, that may count as a change of use. That process starts with a building permit application, then an [occupancy permit](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg), and code upgrades may be needed.
Where an occupancy permit is required, the City must issue it before you see patients in the space.

In Manitoba, X-ray equipment must be registered, and the [X-Ray Safety Regulation](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/regs/current/341-88r.php?lang=en) requires the minister's prior approval, with scaled drawings showing the shielding, before a machine goes into a permanent location. Your professional regulator and equipment suppliers may have their own requirements, so involve them early.

Our guide to [clinic renovation permits in Winnipeg](/blog/clinic-renovation-permits-winnipeg) covers these steps in order. This is general information, not legal advice: the City and your regulator decide what applies to your space.
Building into an existing space
Before signing a lease, check:
Whether the City's zoning allows a clinic in that unit
Where existing plumbing and drains are, since moving them is costly
Electrical capacity for your equipment, and your equipment supplier's installation requirements
Accessibility of the entrance, parking and washrooms
Ceiling height and HVAC capacity
[Asbestos testing](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba) in older buildings before demolition
Walk the space with a contractor before you sign, so you don't end up in one that's expensive to convert.
Minimizing downtime for existing clinics
If you're renovating an operating clinic:
Phase the work room by room
Schedule noisy and dusty work after hours, where the City's [noise rules](https://www.winnipeg.ca/building-development/property-records/construction-your-neighbourhood) allow
Use dust barriers, and negative air where your clinical team or designer calls for it
Keep accessible routes and washrooms open

Phased work also has to respect Manitoba's [Accessible Customer Service Standard](https://accessibilitymb.ca/resources/cs-standard/general/cs-handbook.pdf): existing accessibility features must keep working, and the public must be told when one is out of service.
The bottom line
Successful medical office renovations start with workflow, plan for cleanability and code from day one, and follow a phasing plan the clinic can keep working through.
